issuer: New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department
title: New Mexico TRD Ruling 100-96-3 Application of Section 7-1-26 to Estate
text:
Ruling 100-96-3
Issued: November 25, 1996
Effective: November 25, 1996
Revised: December 5, 2008, citations updated, as indicated by brackets
A ruling has been requested concerning the applicability of certain provisions of the Tax
Administration Act to the following facts:
X died September 5, 1992. The Co-Personal Representatives of X's estate (“Estate”)
filed a federal estate tax return and a New Mexico estate tax report in August 1993
and paid substantial estate taxes to both the Internal Revenue Service (“IRS”) and
the New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department (“Department”).
The Estate filed its first fiduciary income tax return for a period ending July 31,
1993, paying the New Mexico fiduciary income tax due. A significant portion of this
tax represented capital gains from the sale of Estate assets. Pursuant to federal and
New Mexico law, the amount of gain was calculated by comparing the selling price
of the assets to the value of the assets on the date of X's death.
The IRS subsequently audited the Estate's federal estate tax return. After
determining that some estate assets had been undervalued, the IRS assessed
additional estate tax. The Co-Personal Representatives disagreed with the IRS's
determination of value and filed a petition in the United States Tax Court. That
petition is still pending.
If the IRS prevails, the Estate will owe additional estate taxes to the federal
government and to the State of New Mexico. At the same time, the Estate will be
entitled to a refund of federal and New Mexico income tax for the year ending July
31, 1993. This is because an increase in the date-of-death value of estate assets for
estate tax purposes will decrease the amount of capital gain the Estate must
recognize for income tax purposes.
In order to prevent its potential refund of income tax from being barred by the statute
of limitations, the Estate filed protective refund claims with the IRS and the
Department. In October 1996, the Department returned the refund claim with a
notice advising the Estate that New Mexico does not recognize protective claims.
The Estate asks whether the audit of the Estate's federal estate tax return qualifies as an
“audit” under NMSA 1978, Section 7-1-26(D) [7-1-26(F)], for purposes of extending the time
within which the Estate may file a claim for refund of New Mexico income tax paid for the year
ending July 31, 1993.
Pursuant to Section 7-1-26(B) [7-1-26(D)] NMSA 1978, no refund of tax may be allowed
unless the claim for refund is filed within three years of the end of the calendar year in which
payment of the tax was originally due. Under Subsection B [D], the statute of limitations for

claiming a refund of fiduciary income taxes due for the year ending July 1, 1993, would be
December 31, 1996.
Section 7-1-26(D) [7-1-26(F)] NMSA 1978 provides an extended limitations period for
refund claims based on adjustments of federal tax resulting from an IRS audit:
D. [F.] If, as a result of an audit by the internal revenue service ..., any
adjustment of federal tax is made with the result that there would have been an
overpayment of tax if the adjustment to federal tax had been applied to the taxable
period to which it relates, claim for credit or refund of only that amount based on the
adjustment may be made as provided in this section within one year of the date of
the internal revenue service audit adjustment or payment of the federal refund or
within the period limited by Subsection B [D] of this section, whichever expires later
…
Nothing in Subsection D [F] requires the IRS to audit the specific tax for which the refund
claim is made. Subsection D [F] does require that the claim be based on an adjustment of federal tax
resulting from an IRS audit and that the adjustment apply to the same taxable period for which the
New Mexico refund is sought.
In this case, any adjustment to the Estate's federal income tax liability for the year ending
July 31, 1993, will be a direct result of the IRS audit of the federal estate tax return. If the pending
estate tax litigation is decided in favor of the IRS, the Estate will be able to recover federal income
tax based on the increase in the date-of-death value of X's assets, which is also the basis of those
assets for income tax purposes. The refund of federal income tax will, in turn, trigger the one-year
statute of limitations contained in Subsection D [F] of Section 7-1-26.
Under the facts presented, the Estate will have one year from the date the IRS refunds any
federal income tax the Estate overpaid for the year ended July 31, 1993, within which to file a claim
for refund of New Mexico income tax overpaid for the same period.
